test_cases.title: Confirm there is no keyboard-triggered fault path for Lx (structural/code-review only)
test_cases.skip_reason: Code-review-only finding, re-confirmed against the current app/intersection/src/lx_sensor.c: the only cases in its switch(input) are a/A/c/C/1/2/3/4/w/W/h/?/q, none of which call any fault-raising function. The only place fsm->faults is ever OR'd is lx_fsm_report_watchdog_trip() (lx_fsm.c), whose only caller is lx_watchdog_thread(). There is no keyboard key or IPC verb that raises an Lx fault directly, so there is no runtime behavior for this tool to script - only a static read of the source proves this.

test_cases.title: FAULT_SAFE always wins - every new command NACKs with FAULT_ACTIVE once Lx is faulted (runtime blocked on watchdog trip)
test_cases.skip_reason: The runtime portion requires L1 to already be in SUPERVISORY_FAULT_SAFE. Per TC-FAULT-11, lx_sensor.c has no keyboard key that raises a fault - the only way in is a real watchdog trip (Group 5), which itself needs a debugger able to stall only the server thread while lx_watchdog_thread() keeps running (see TC-FAULT-17's caveat). This keystroke-only automation tool cannot create that precondition, so it cannot exercise lx_fsm_on_set_mode()/lx_fsm_on_set_timing_profile()/lx_fsm_on_request_override() NACKing with FAULT_ACTIVE. The doc's code-review half (that lx_fsm_check_fault_locked() gates every lx_fsm_on_*() handler except lx_fsm_on_crossing_status()) is a static-analysis verdict with no distinguishing runtime output to check.

test_cases.title: FAULT_SAFE forcibly terminates an active REQUEST_OVERRIDE (SC-03A) (runtime blocked on watchdog trip)
test_cases.skip_reason: Same precondition problem as TC-FAULT-12: entering SUPERVISORY_FAULT_SAFE while override_substate == OVR_ACTIVE requires a real Lx watchdog trip, only reachable via a debugger that can freeze just the server thread (TC-FAULT-17) - lx_sensor.c has no keyboard fault trigger (TC-FAULT-11). Without that trip this tool cannot exercise lx_fsm_report_watchdog_trip()'s call to lx_fsm_terminate_override_locked(); the code-review fallback (lx_fsm.c's fsm->supervisory == SUPERVISORY_CENTRAL_OVERRIDE check inside that function) has nothing to run.

test_cases.title: FAULT_SAFE does not block MSG_CROSSING_STATUS replies (Lx only observes, never rejects) (code review only)
test_cases.skip_reason: Pure code-review verdict: lx_fsm_on_crossing_status() always sets reply->result = RESULT_ACK regardless of fsm->supervisory (per its RC-02 comment), so there is no NACK/ACK branch difference a log-pattern check could distinguish at runtime. The doc itself flags the full runtime variant (a live neighboring RLx plus a tripped Lx watchdog at the same time) as an unnecessary complex combination, not required to demonstrate this - reading lx_fsm.c is sufficient and is what this finding is actually based on.

test_cases.title: REQUEST_FAULT_CLEAR resumes Lx from FAULT_SAFE to NORMAL_OPERATION when the neighboring crossing is OPEN (runtime blocked on watchdog trip)
test_cases.skip_reason: Precondition (L1 already SUPERVISORY_FAULT_SAFE) can only be reached via a real watchdog trip, which needs a debugger able to stall only the server thread while lx_watchdog_thread() keeps running (TC-FAULT-17) - lx_sensor.c has no fault-triggering key (TC-FAULT-11). Without that precondition this tool cannot keystroke its way to exercising lx_fsm_on_request_fault_clear()'s ACK path, even though the clear request itself (C1's 'f' -> node type '0' -> Lx number) is otherwise fully keyboard-driven.

test_cases.title: REQUEST_FAULT_CLEAR resumes RAILWAY_PREEMPTION (not NORMAL_OPERATION) when the neighboring crossing is still closed (safety regression case; runtime blocked on watchdog trip)
test_cases.skip_reason: Same debugger-dependent precondition as TC-FAULT-14b (a real Lx watchdog trip is required to enter FAULT_SAFE while fsm->last_crossing_state != CROSSING_OPEN), plus this case additionally needs a live neighboring rlx_main actually driving real MSG_CROSSING_STATUS updates timed against the trip - not reachable through this tool's keystroke-only automation. Verify instead by code review of lx_fsm_on_request_fault_clear() in app/intersection/src/lx_fsm.c: 'fsm->supervisory = (fsm->last_crossing_state != CROSSING_OPEN) ? SUPERVISORY_RAILWAY_PREEMPTION : SUPERVISORY_NORMAL_OPERATION;'

test_cases.title: Watchdog dead-man's-switch logic confirmed by code review (baseline for Group 5, always passes without a QNX machine)
test_cases.skip_reason: This is explicitly a code-review case, not a runtime one (per the .md: 'Loai: review code, khong phai runtime'). It reads lx_watchdog_thread() (app/intersection/src/lx_watchdog.c) and rlx_watchdog_thread() (app/railway/src/rlx_watchdog.c) to confirm each runs sleep()-then-compare-counter loops on their own dedicated thread and calls lx_fsm_report_watchdog_trip()/rlx_fsm_report_watchdog_trip() independently of the server thread. There is no keystroke input or log pattern this tool can assert beyond what TC-FAULT-17/18 already attempt at runtime.

test_cases.title: Negative proof: kill -STOP/-CONT on the whole process does NOT trigger the watchdog (documents why this approach is invalid for PA-10)
test_cases.skip_reason: This case is about sending POSIX signals (SIGSTOP/SIGCONT) to a running node's PID mid-test. runner.py's NodeProcess only supports scripted stdin keystrokes (steps[].send) and terminate() at cleanup - it has no facility to send OS signals to a running node process. Even if it did, the .md's own analysis (confirmed against the multi-threaded design of lx_watchdog.c/rlx_watchdog.c) explains that SIGSTOP/SIGCONT act on the whole process including the watchdog thread itself, so the watchdog would never observe a 'gap' - this test is a deliberate negative result, not something worth adding signal-delivery machinery to reproduce.

test_cases.title: Best-effort: trip the Lx watchdog via a debugger that stalls only the server thread
test_cases.skip_reason: Requires a debugger (gdb / QNX Momentics) capable of stopping only the server thread (e.g. via a breakpoint inside the phase-timer handling path in lx_fsm.c/lx_main.c) while lx_watchdog_thread() keeps running on its own thread for at least LX_WATCHDOG_CHECK_INTERVAL_S*2 (4s). This keystroke-only automation tool has no per-thread stop/continue capability and cannot attach a debugger, so it cannot script this. Per the .md's own caveat, even manual attempts may fail on debug tooling that stops every thread at a breakpoint (the same problem as TC-FAULT-16) - TC-FAULT-15's code review is the fallback evidence.

test_cases.title: Best-effort: trip the RLx watchdog via a debugger that stalls only the server thread (gate must be commanded closed even while fully idle/OPEN)
test_cases.skip_reason: Same debugger-only limitation as TC-FAULT-17, applied to rlx_main's server thread (a breakpoint inside rlx_fsm_on_tick(), app/railway/src/rlx_fsm.c) while rlx_watchdog_thread() keeps running for at least RLX_WATCHDOG_CHECK_INTERVAL_S*2 (6s). This tool has no debugger/per-thread-stall capability. Fallback evidence is TC-FAULT-15's code review plus TC-FAULT-01/04's confirmation that enter_fault() unconditionally commands the gate closed.

test_cases.title: Stuck pedestrian button (repeated/held press) does not set FAULT_PED_BUTTON_STUCK - accepted PoC limitation, confirmed not to hang the WALK/FDW sequence

checks.description: cold-start phase is PHASE_ARTERIAL_GREEN (compatible with side 0/1 per lx_fsm.c's ASSUMPTION comment), so the first latched press starts a WALK sequence almost immediately

LX_WALK_MS(6s)+LX_FLASHING_DONT_WALK_MS(4s)=10s later the sequence completes to DONT_WALK despite continuous simulated 'holding' of the button (repeated '1' presses every 2s) - proves lx_fsm_latch_pedestrian_request()'s coalescing (ped_recall) does not hang or infinite-loop under a stuck-style input. There is no printed FAULT_PED_BUTTON_STUCK message to check for in either direction (by design, per lx_fsm.c's own comment: 'FAULT_PED_BUTTON_STUCK ... is never set by this file') - this is a code-confirmed limitation, not something a missing-pattern check could additionally verify.

test_cases.title: Stuck vehicle sensor (arterial demand held forever, never cleared) does not set FAULT_VEHICLE_SENSOR_STUCK - accepted PoC limitation, confirmed system keeps cycling normally

checks.description: cold start is MODE_PEAK_FIXED (no Central in environment A to send SET_MODE to MODE_OFF_PEAK_SENSOR), so LX_CYCLE_LENGTH_MS (90s: 48+4+2+30+4+2) elapses on a fixed schedule regardless of arterial_vehicle_demand. The very first 'SIGNAL -> ARTERIAL GREEN' print happens at process cold-start, before this check's since_monotonic cutoff (t0, set after setup_wait_ms) - so this check only matches the SECOND arterial-green entry, one full 90s cycle later, proving the intersection keeps cycling normally (never freezes into FAULT_SAFE) even though fsm->arterial_vehicle_demand has been held at 1 with 'A' never pressed. As with TC-FAULT-19, there is no FAULT_VEHICLE_SENSOR_STUCK printf to check for - lx_fsm.c has no elapsed-time-since-asserted tracking for this demand flag at all, by design.

test_cases.title: Stuck train-approaching sensor (repeated '0' before the 5s warning timer elapses) does not reset the closing timer or set FAULT_TRAIN_SENSOR_STUCK - accepted PoC limitation

checks.pattern: RLx: commanding gates DOWN \(simulated motion, 3000 ms\)
checks.description: RLX_WARNING case in rlx_fsm_simulate_train_approaching() only calls register_window() again on a repeated '0' (self-loop) - it does NOT reset fsm->state_elapsed_ms. If repeated presses incorrectly reset the timer, enter_closing() would only fire at ~4000+5000=9000ms after the LAST press; instead it fires at ~5000ms after the FIRST press (within this check's 6500ms budget), proving the 'stuck sensor' repeated-approach signal does not delay closing. RLX_WARNING_DIAGNOSTIC_TIMEOUT_MS (60s, rlx_timer.h) exists but is RESERVED/unreferenced, and no FAULT_TRAIN_SENSOR_STUCK printf exists anywhere in rlx_fsm.c/rlx_gate.c to check for - confirmed by code review as well as this runtime timing check.
